input: Liquid-liquid extraction is an attractive and widely used separation technique, and in the present work it was applied to the recovery of acetone from an aqueous stream by contacting the stream with an organic solvent into which the acetone preferentially dissolves. The performance of any such extraction is governed to a considerable extent by the distribution coefficient, which expresses the ratio in which the solute divides itself between the two liquid phases at equilibrium, and for the system studied here the distribution coefficient of acetone, defined as the concentration in the organic phase over the concentration in the aqueous phase, has a value of 1.33 at a temperature of 25 °C. Building on this foundation, the design of the extraction unit makes use of 8 countercurrent stages, an arrangement in which the two liquid streams flow in opposite directions through the cascade so that the driving force for transfer is maintained from stage to stage. On the basis of the design calculations, the predicted recovery of acetone is 89% of the acetone that is present in the feed, which represents a substantial degree of removal. It is important to appreciate, however, that this prediction rests on certain assumptions that underpin the calculation, most notably the assumption that every stage behaves as an equilibrium stage and the assumption that the mutual solubility of the two solvents is negligible. Neither of these assumptions has yet been checked against the actual solvents that would be used, and so the figure of 89% should be regarded as a prediction whose reliability remains to be confirmed rather than as an established performance figure.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient, the concentration of acetone in the organic phase over its concentration in the aqueous phase at equilibrium, is 1.33 at 25 °C. The design uses 8 countercurrent stages, in which the two phases pass in opposite directions and each phase leaves against the freshest portion of the other. Predicted recovery is 89% of the acetone in the feed. Recovery is stated on the acetone in the feed: it is the share of the feed's acetone that leaves in the organic phase. The distribution coefficient is a property of the two solvents and the solute at the stated temperature, and the stage count is where the design spends it, stage by stage against the incoming feed. A measured recovery on the actual solvents would test both assumptions together, since each moves the result away from the prediction in a different part of the cascade. The prediction carries its assumptions inside it. It assumes that each stage reaches equilibrium, so the streams leaving a stage stand in the ratio the distribution coefficient fixes, and it assumes that the mutual solubility of the two solvents is negligible, so neither phase gains or loses volume to the other as the acetone moves. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. The direction of the exposure is known for the first assumption: a stage that falls short of equilibrium transfers less acetone than the calculation credits to it, so recovery in operation falls below 89% for the same stage count, by an amount the prediction does not state. The second assumption, if it fails, changes the phase flows themselves, and with them the stage-to-stage balance on which the predicted recovery rests. The predicted recovery is therefore a design figure, conditional on equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility, and it awaits a check on the actual solvents before it can be read as expected performance.
